claims.text: Untreated high-value alloy components are subject to oxidation, wear, and other degradation under aggressive operating conditions.
Laser cladding can deposit a nanostructured ceramic composite coating onto an alloy surface.
The proposed coating may contain TiC or Al2O3 particulates in a metallic binder.
The intervention is intended for high-temperature, oxidative, and mechanically wearing environments.
The coating must remain adherent and stable under repeated thermal and mechanical stresses to remain effective.
Hard ceramic particulates in a well-bonded metallic matrix create a composite microstructure that resists deformation.
Hard ceramic particulates in a well-bonded metallic matrix inhibit crack propagation.
Hard ceramic particulates in a well-bonded metallic matrix increase wear resistance.
Laser cladding produces a metallurgically bonded coating.
Laser cladding reinforces the surface with high-hardness phases and a refined microstructure.
The resulting coating acts as a barrier against oxidation.
The resulting coating resists mechanical wear and delays surface degradation relative to an untreated surface.
Coated components will have greater surface hardness than untreated components during simulated aggressive-environment testing.
Coated components will have a lower wear rate than untreated components during simulated aggressive-environment testing.
The intervention may lose effectiveness above the thermal-stability limit of the coating.
Poor coating adhesion may cause premature delamination and limit effectiveness.
Performance depends on the balance between ceramic and metallic coating constituents.
The magnitude of improvement depends on coating composition, laser-cladding parameters, and substrate compatibility.
